The third-party remitter controls all remedies. The payee, whose name and address are physically printed on the instrument, is invisible to the bank 's intake system. This complaint documents what happens when that gap meets a live instrument with a compromised custody history and a payee who had no way to protect her identity. The underlying transaction was an entity disbursement. I am not asking the CFPB to review the originating entity 's internal governance, administrative rights, or entitlement to funds. I am strictly asking the CFPB to review what U.S. Bank did and failed to do after one of its own official checks entered circulation bearing my identity. What Happened Official Check # XXXX was issued in my name on XX/XX/year>, and mailed via regular USPS First-Class Mail without tracking, without mailing confirmation, and without my knowledge or consent. I was not consulted about how the instrument would be sent. I was not informed until it was already in circulation. A {$5000.00} negotiable instrument bearing my legal name and mailing address entered the public mail stream with zero accountability infrastructure and zero input from the person whose identity was on it. It never arrived. On XX/XX/year> On Day 15 following issuance, I contacted U.S. Bank 's Fraud Liaison Unit not to obtain account information, but to provide it. The Fraud Liaison refused to open a case. No check number was requested. No intake occurred. No mechanism existed for a named payee to submit risk information about an active instrument bearing her own identity. I then filed reports with the USPS Postal Inspection Service and local law enforcement. On XX/XX/year> I executed a notarized Affidavit of Non-Receipt and Non-Negotiation and presented it personally at a U.S. Bank branch in XXXX, California. No intake occurred. XX/XX/XXXX XX/XX/year> I contacted multiple U.S. Bank personnel by email. No substantive response was received. On XX/XX/year> I was informed by the originating remitter without documentation that the instrument had been returned to sender, that a stop-payment had been initiated, that the stop-payment had been reversed, and that the same compromised instrument had been re-mailed. I was not asked. I was not notified in advance. I can not help but consider whether earlier bank intervention, had any reporting mechanism existed, might have prevented that second circulation entirely. The bank 's structural blind spot removed the only friction that might have stopped it. When the instrument arrived by Certified Mail on XX/XX/XXXX, I was handed an impossible choice. Accept it and contradict my sworn affidavit, waive all objections to the 29-day custody gap, and absorb every unresolved risk alone. Or refuse it, and watch the instrument re-enter circulation, my PII remain exposed, and control return to the party that created the problem. I refused. There was no option that protected me. On XX/XX/year> I contacted the Fraud Liaison Unit again. Still no meaningful intake occurred. Later that day, I reached branch personnel directly at the issuing location for the first time. I submitted affidavits, police reports, USPIS confirmation, and a complete chronology. U.S. Bank 's Executive Communications unit acknowledged receipt twice, in identical language, and provided no substantive response either time. The Harm I can not prove the instrument was intercepted, copied, or washed during those 29 days. Neither can anyone else. That uncertainty does not resolve in my favor ; it lives on my shoulders indefinitely. I am not the bank 's account holder. I am not the remitter. I am the person whose legal name and address are printed on a {$5000.00} negotiable instrument that floated untracked and unsecured through the public mail stream for nearly a month without my consent and without any mechanism for me to report the risk. If my PII was compromised during that window, no replacement check cures it. No cancellation retrieves a photographed document. No internal electronic status change eliminates the risk the physical paper continues to represent. The instrument is currently in transit back to the originating party. It has sat processing at a USPS facility since XX/XX/XXXX. When it arrives, I have no visibility into what happens next. The same parties who sent it untracked the first time, who facilitated re-circulation without documentation or payee consent, will have it back in their possession. Nothing has changed structurally to prevent this cycle from repeating. My exposure is not past tense. It is ongoing and I have no mechanism to stop it. I made contact with U.S. Bank across every available channelFraud Liaison, branch walk-in, multiple emails, a second Fraud Liaison call, direct branch contact at the issuing location, and Executive Communications escalation across nearly two months. I filed law enforcement reports. I executed a sworn affidavit. I submitted documentation at the bank 's own request. I did everything available to me. U.S. Bank has never confirmed whether any of it mattered. SEE ATTACHED DOCUMENT " FULL_COMPLAINT_TEXT.PDF '' FOR EVIDENCE AND EXHIBITS.

XXXX further stated that the account was referred to collections after being in delinquent status for so long. Yet neither XXXX nor Aldous has produced any documentation demonstrating what efforts were made to communicate with me during that period. The only documentation provided by Aldous is a copy of the original membership agreement signed in XX/XX/XXXX. While this document may demonstrate that a membership once existed, it does not verify the accuracy of the reported balance, the amount claimed, the communications allegedly sent, the collection referral process, or the adequacy of the investigation performed after my dispute. I respectfully request that the CFPB require Aldous & Associates to provide competent documentation supporting : 1. The balance being reported ; 2. The calculation of the amount claimed ; 3. The basis for continuing to report this account despite my documented attempt to obtain a cancellation form prior to collection activity. A " reasonable reinvestigation '' requires more than forwarding a dispute to the furnisher via the automated e-OSCAR system and accepting their response. For accounts where Equifax has previously returned a conclusory " meets FCRA requirement '' finding without providing documentation of what reinvestigation method was used or what information was exchanged, those responses do not satisfy the reasonable reinvestigation standard established under Cushman v. An incorrect SSN raises the risk of a mixed file another consumer 's accounts being attributed to my file or mine to theirs and Equifax is obligated to conduct a mixed file review. WHAT I WANT : I am requesting the CFPB require Equifax to : ( 1 ) conduct genuine reinvestigations of all disputed accounts listed above, not simply relay disputes to furnishers via automated systems ; ( 2 ) delete any account where the furnisher can not verify accuracy within the required 30-day window ; ( 3 ) correct my Social Security Number on file and conduct a mixed file review; and ( 4 ) provide written results of all reinvestigations as required by FCRA 611 ( a ) ( 6 ).

Summary : Rocket closed my refinance using a payoff of {$790000.00} and disclosed I owed {$970.00} at closing. Weeks later Rocket demanded an additional ~ {$5900.00} due to an alleged payoff shortage that was never disclosed before closing. Story : In XX/XX/year>, I completed a VA Interest Rate Reduction Refinance Loan ( IRRRL ) with Rocket Mortgage. Prior to closing, Rocket Mortgage provided a payoff amount for my existing Rocket Mortgage loan and prepared the final closing documents based on that payoff amount. I reviewed and signed the final Closing Disclosure and closing package. The documents showed a payoff to my existing mortgage of approximately {$790000.00} and a borrower cash-to-close amount of less than {$1000.00}. Based on the final signed closing documents, I proceeded with the refinance and believed the transaction was complete. After the refinance closed and funded, I was contacted by Rocket Mortgage and informed that there was an alleged payoff shortage. On XX/XX/year>, Rocket Mortgage sent an email stating there was a payoff shortage of {$5400.00} due to a tax disbursement that was not included in the payoff used at closing. Rocket Mortgage requested immediate payment and stated that interest would continue to accrue daily until the amount was paid. The following day, the amount demanded increased to approximately {$5800.00} due to additional interest charges. I am filing this complaint because I do not believe Rocket Mortgage adequately disclosed this potential liability before closing. The final Closing Disclosure and signed closing package reflected a substantially lower amount due from me. Rocket Mortgage was both the lender being paid off and the lender originating the refinance, and the closing was handled through an affiliated Rocket entity. Despite this, I was later informed that the payoff amount used at closing was allegedly incorrect. To date, I have requested a detailed reconciliation showing : The payoff quote used at closing. The date the payoff quote was generated. The specific tax disbursement that allegedly created the shortage. How the alleged shortage amount was calculated. Why the issue was not identified and resolved before closing. My concern is not only the amount being demanded, but also that I relied on Rocket Mortgage 's final closing documents when deciding to complete the refinance. I believe consumers should be able to rely on the final figures presented at closing. I am requesting that Rocket Mortgage provide a complete accounting of the alleged shortage, explain why the discrepancy was not identified before closing, and review whether it is appropriate to hold the borrower responsible for costs resulting from an apparent payoff calculation or closing process error.

During the calls, Chase representatives gave inconsistent and confusing explanations about whether the matter could even be processed. One representative stated that the matter would be transferred to claims to report this, get investigated, and also get the funds back, and also stated that the transaction and reason for dispute had already been placed on file. A later representative then told me that the dispute was not going through, that Chase was unable to reverse it because it was an authorized self-payment, that there was no debit card involved, that XXXX was a third party, that Chase had no recovery rights for XXXX payments , and that Regulation E did not apply because my card was not involved. Despite those statements, the same representative also stated, Ive gone ahead and filed a claim. The claim then appeared in the Chase portal, was shown as opened, and was closed the same day. That sequence is exactly why I am complaining. Chases handling appears contradictory, perfunctory, and misleading. If Chases position is that it will not honor this type of claim, then it should say so clearly, consistently, and based on an identifiable written policy. Instead, I received a series of shifting explanations that suggested the representatives themselves were either improvising, misapplying policy, or attempting to discourage or narrow the complaint before it could be fully reviewed. The fact that the claim was both said to be non-viable and nevertheless filed, then closed the same day, raises serious concerns about whether Chase performed any meaningful review at all. I am also concerned about misleading signals created by Chases own payment flow and prior oral statements. Chases XXXX interface asked me to identify the nature or purpose of the payment, including a service-related classification, which reasonably suggested that the nature of the transaction could matter for risk review, complaint handling, or dispute processing. I was also previously told by a Chase employee that there was a much longer period in which claims could be raised. Later, however, Chase representatives told me that authorized XXXX disputes involving service issues, non-performance, or similar problems effectively would not be processed. If Chase collects purpose-of-payment information but later treats that classification as meaningless when a consumer seeks help, that is misleading. If Chase representatives are telling consumers materially different things about what is reviewable, what deadlines exist, and whether any complaint path exists at all, that is also misleading. I want Chase to provide a clear written explanation of the following : what the purpose-of-payment classification in the XXXX flow actually means ; whether Chase has a formal complaint, escalation, or review process for authorized XXXX payments involving deception , fake or misleading contract representations, non-performance, or service-related disputes ; the exact written policy basis for the statements I received that the claim could not go through ; why I was told the matter would be investigated and put on file, only for Chase to later say it was not viable while still filing the claim ; why the claim was opened and closed the same day ; whether any evidence review occurred before closure ; whether the recorded calls will be preserved and reviewed ; and whether the representatives involved were following written policy or giving incorrect and improvised explanations. To be clear, I did not present this to Chase as a routine buyers remorse issue. I reported it as a scam or deceptive-inducement situation involving a purported sublease, a purported contract used to create a false sense of legitimacy, and representations that caused me to authorize the payment under false pretenses. Chases handling of that report was inconsistent from start to finish and did not provide a clear, fair, or transparent complaint process. The portal also stated that Chase had sent a letter detailing the outcome, but no outcome letter or attached decision document was available to me in the claim or notices area at the time I checked. I am asking CFPB to require Chase to review this matter properly, preserve and review the recorded calls, provide a written explanation addressing the contradictions described above, and explain whether Chases current intake and handling of these XXXX complaints is misleading to consumers.

Consumer complaint narrative: I am writing to dispute a charged-off account that is showing up on my Experian credit report from XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX located at XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXXXXXX XXXX I believe this account is being reported inaccurately in XXXX specific ways, and I am asking the CFPB to investigate and asking Experian to correct or delete this account. Here is the account information : Creditor : XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX Account Number : XXXX Account Type : Deposit account Date Opened : XX/XX/XXXX Date of Charge-Off : XX/XX/XXXX Balance Reported : {$4200.00} Status on my report : Account charged off, {$4200.00} written off, listed as {$4200.00} past due as of XX/XX/XXXX I have two main problems with how this account is being reported, and I want to explain both of them. Problem 1 The balance has not changed even though the account was charged off over 3 years ago This account was charged off in XX/XX/XXXX. That means XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX wrote off this debt more than three years ago. But my credit report still shows the exact same balance of {$4200.00} with no change at all. That does not make sense because once an account is charged off, the creditor is supposed to update how they report the balance. They can not just leave the same number sitting there forever as if nothing happened. Under the Fair Credit Reporting Act, specifically 15 U.S.C. Section 1681s-2 ( b ), companies that report information to credit bureaus are required to make sure that information is accurate and up to date. When an account is charged off, the creditor takes a tax write-off on that amount. After that happens, continuing to report the same unchanged balance as if it is still growing or still owed in the same way is misleading. I am asking Experian and the CFPB to require XXXX to either update this balance to reflect what is accurate today, or to remove the account entirely. Problem 2 The report says the account is still 'past due as of XX/XX/XXXX ' but it was charged off in XX/XX/XXXX My Experian report shows this account as " {$4200.00} past due as of XX/XX/XXXX. ' That language makes it look like this account just became past due recently, but that is not what happened. This account charged off back in XX/XX/XXXX, which is over three years ago. The 'past due as of " date should reflect when the account actually went delinquent, not keep updating every single month to make it look like something new is happening. This is a known problem with how some creditors report charged-off accounts. When a creditor keeps refreshing the 'past due as of " date on an old charge-off, it makes the negative item look much more recent than it actually is. That is unfair and inaccurate because it makes my credit report look worse than the real situation. The FCRA, under Section 1681s-2 ( b ), requires that furnishers report accurate information. Saying an account that charged off in XXXX is 'past due as of XX/XX/XXXX ' is misleading and inaccurate, and it needs to be corrected. Also, my report shows this account with charge-off codes ( 'CO ' ) all the way from early XXXX through XX/XX/XXXX every single month for over three years. There is no explanation of why the status and the past-due date keep getting updated on a closed, written-off account. Under FCRA Section 1681c, most negative items can only stay on a credit report for seven years from the date of first delinquency. Updating the reported date could also affect when this account is supposed to come off my report, which would be another violation. What I am asking for : I am asking the CFPB to look into how XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX is reporting this account, and I am asking Experian to investigate it under their obligations in the FCRA. Specifically I want : Experian to investigate this account under FCRA Section 1681i and contact FirstLight to verify whether the balance and past-due date are being reported accurately ; The 'past due as of XX/XX/XXXX ' language to be corrected to reflect the actual date this account first went delinquent not a continuously refreshed current date ; The balance to be updated to accurately reflect the status of this account post-charge-off, or for the account to be deleted if FirstLight can not verify the accuracy of what they are reporting ; Written notice of the results of this investigation within 30 days as required by FCRA Section 1681i ( a ) ( 1 ) ( A ) ; If this account can not be verified as completely accurate, it must be deleted from my Experian credit report under FCRA Section 1681i ( a ) ( 5 ) ( A ). Why this matters to me : Having this account reported the way it is makes my credit look worse than it should. The way the past-due date keeps updating makes lenders think this is a recent problem when it is actually from XXXX. That is hurting my ability to get credit, better interest rates, and other financial products I need. I am not trying to make a legitimate debt disappear I am asking for it to be reported in a way that is actually accurate and fair, which is what the law requires. I am also sending a copy of this letter and my credit report directly to XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. They are a local credit union here in XXXX XXXX and I believe they may be willing to work with me to correct this if contacted directly. However, I want this formal complaint on record with the CFPB regardless. If this is not resolved correctly, I am prepared to look into further options available to me under the FCRA, including FCRA Sections 1681n and 1681o, which allow consumers to seek damages for willful or negligent noncompliance by creditors or credit bureaus.

Monthly payment is listed as " No Info '' despite this being a 74-month installment loan with established payment terms. -- - ACCOUNT XXXX : XXXX ( XXXX XXXX ) -- - Status : Charge-off. This account contains a direct internal contradiction : it reports a Current Payment Status of " Charge-off '' while simultaneously showing XXXX XXXX days late as XXXX. A charge-off is legally impossible without prior delinquency these XXXX data points can not coexist. Additionally, the payment history shows " Unknown '' for every single month of XXXX and XXXX over two full years of missing data. The account remarks reflect " Account information disputed by consumer '' TWICE, meaning two prior disputes were filed and neither produced a documented resolution or written results as required by FCRA 611 ( a ) ( 6 ). -- - ACCOUNT XXXX : XXXX XXXX ( Telecommunications/Collection ) -- - Status : In Collections. This account also contains a direct internal contradiction : Current Payment Status of " In Collections '' while Times 30/60/90+ days late = XXXX. A collection account can not exist with XXXX days of delinquency at any threshold. The remarks reflect " Account information disputed by consumer '' TWICE two prior unresolved disputes. Large portions of the XXXX payment history show " Unknown. '' -- - ACCOUNT 4 & 5 : XXXX XXXX XXXX ( Two Collection Accounts ) -- - Both XXXX accounts one for XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX ( {$9800.00}, XXXX opened XX/XX/XXXX ; original delinquency XX/XX/XXXX ) and one for XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX ( {$880.00}, XXXX opened XX/XX/XXXX ; original delinquency XX/XX/XXXX ) show " Account information disputed by consumer '' TWICE each. Four combined unresolved dispute notations across two accounts, with no documented reinvestigation results provided for any of them. Both accounts also present potential re-aging concerns under FCRA 605 ( c ), as XXXX 's " Date Opened '' significantly post-dates the original dates of first delinquency. FCRA VIOLATIONS BY TRANSUNION : 1. FAILURE TO CONDUCT REASONABLE REINVESTIGATION [ FCRA 611 ( a ) ( 1 ) ] : Multiple accounts show " Account information disputed by consumer '' appearing TWICE meaning TransUnion has processed at least two dispute cycles per account without correcting the identified inaccuracies. For the XXXX XXXX and XXXX accounts, the inaccuracies are internal contradictions within TransUnion 's own data a charge-off with XXXX late payments and a collection with 0/0/0 late payments. A genuine reinvestigation would have flagged these contradictions immediately. The fact that they remain uncorrected after multiple dispute cycles demonstrates that TransUnion is not conducting reasonable reinvestigations as required by FCRA 611 ( a ) ( 1 ). 2. RUBBER-STAMPING FURNISHER RESPONSES : The pattern of returning " Account information disputed by consumer '' notations without correction suggests TransUnion is forwarding disputes to furnishers via the automated e-OSCAR system and accepting their responses without independent review of the accuracy of the reported data. Courts have consistently held that this practice does not constitute a " reasonable reinvestigation '' under the FCRA. XXXX. FAILURE TO PROVIDE WRITTEN REINVESTIGATION RESULTS [ FCRA 611 ( a ) ( 6 ) ] : Despite multiple dispute cycles across multiple accounts, I have not received written results of completed reinvestigations as required by FCRA 611 ( a ) ( 6 ). 4. MAINTAINING INTERNALLY CONTRADICTORY DATA [ FCRA 607 ( b ) ] : TransUnion has an independent obligation under FCRA 607 ( b ) to maintain reasonable procedures to assure maximum possible accuracy of the information it reports. The presence of accounts showing charge-off or collection status with XXXX days of delinquency represents a failure of those reasonable accuracy procedures. 5. NAME DISCREPANCY / POTENTIAL MIXED FILE : My TransUnion report shows my name as " XXXX XXXX XXXX '' a middle name variation not present on my XXXX or XXXX reports. Combined with an incorrect Social Security Number on my other bureau files, this raises concern about potential mixed file issues that TransUnion has an obligation to investigate and resolve. Under standard creditor and regulatory practice, a charge-off requires a sustained period of non-payment typically 120 to 180 days past due. It is legally and factually impossible for an account to carry a charge-off status while simultaneously having zero days of delinquency recorded. One of these two data points must be fabricated or erroneous. Possible Finance is reporting both simultaneously, which constitutes materially inaccurate reporting under FCRA 623 ( a ) ( 1 ). 2. OVER TWO YEARS OF MISSING PAYMENT HISTORY : The payment history grid shows " Unknown '' for every single month of XXXX and every single month of XXXX a gap of 24 consecutive months of missing data. For a derogatory account, the absence of this data prevents any accurate assessment of the account 's history. If this data exists and was not provided to XXXX, Possible Finance has failed its obligation under FCRA 623 to furnish complete and accurate information. 3. FAILURE TO INVESTIGATE AFTER TWO DISPUTES : The account remarks reflect " Account information disputed by consumer '' appearing twice confirming two separate prior consumer disputes were filed. Despite two dispute cycles spanning an extended period, the internal contradiction described in point 1 above remains uncorrected on my XXXX report. Possible Finance had an independent obligation under FCRA 623 ( b ) to review all relevant dispute information and correct inaccurate data. The continued reporting of a charge-off alongside XXXX late payments after two disputes demonstrates a failure to conduct any genuine reinvestigation. 4. IRREGULAR ACCOUNT TIMELINE : This account was open for only 38 days ( XX/XX/XXXX to XX/XX/XXXX ) yet carries a charge-off status with a remaining balance of {$150.00} ( {$240.00} highest balance ). A charge-off on a 38-day-old account with zero reported delinquencies requires documented verification from the furnisher of the exact basis for the charge-off classification. WHAT I WANT : I am requesting the CFPB require Possible Finance to : ( 1 ) reconcile the charge-off status with the XXXX late payment record one must be corrected or the account deleted; ( 2 ) provide complete payment history for XXXX and XXXX, or delete the account if complete data can not be furnished ; ( 3 ) provide documentation of what reinvestigation was conducted in response to each of the two prior disputes ; ( 4 ) provide an itemized explanation of the basis for the charge-off classification given the 38-day account lifespan and zero delinquencies. Consumer complaint narrative: I am a consumer with an account at Synchrony Bank/Synchrony Financial . This is reinforced by the Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002, which strengthens requ irements for accurate books and records and internal accounting controls sufficient to provide reasonable assurance regarding the reliability of financial reporting and the maintenance of accountability for assets. Under the Bank Secrecy Act ( 31 U.S.C. 5311 et seq. ) and its implementing regulations, financial institutions must maintain customer account records, including statements, ledger cards, or other records showing each transaction in or with respect to customer accounts. These records must generally be retained for at least XXXX years and kept in a manner that makes them accessible in a reasonable period of time. Synchronys claim that they do not have or can not produce the full accounting ledger especially after I explicitly rejected statements and demanded the detailed ledger appears inconsistent with these fundamental record-keeping obligations. Their failure to maintain and provide these required records upon proper request constitutes an unfair or deceptive act or practice that has prejudiced me as a consumer. It has prevented me from fully verifying the transactions, balance, and activity on my own account and has hindered my ability to fairly litigate and resolve disputes related to the account. I respectfully request that the CFPB investigate Synchronys record-keeping practices and systems with respect to customer accounting ledgers and transaction records. Specifically, I ask that the CFPB require Synchrony to : 1. Produce the full accounting ledger ( or a complete reconstruction of all transactions and account activity ) for my account, or provide a detailed, sworn explanation of exactly why they can not do so despite their legal obligations under the Securities Exchange Act, Sarbanes-Oxley Act, and Bank Secrecy Act and despite my explicit rejection of statements in favor of the full ledger. XXXX. Explain what searches were conducted, what systems were reviewed, and why records that the law requires them to maintain and keep are allegedly unavailable. XXXX. Take any other appropriate action to ensure compliance with federal record-keeping requirements and to remedy the harm caused to consumers by such failures. I have attached supporting documentation, including a timeline of my requests ( showing my specific demand for the full ledger and rejection of statements ), copies of relevant communications and court filings ( redacted as necessary ), and the responses received from Synchrony. Thank you for your attention to this matter. I look forward to Synchronys response and any investigation or resolution the CFPB deems appropriate.

FDR voids settlements I am funding, lets the full debt be reinstated, then renegotiates and charges a second fee on the same debt.
FDRs own contract defines a settlement as the settlement, reduction, or other change to the terms of an enrolled debt (Section 1.a), and earns its fee only when a settlement is reached on that debt, you authorize the settlement, and at least one payment is made toward that settlement (Sections 1.a and 5.a). Section 4.a admits that when a settlement lapses, the creditor will reject or terminate the settlement, reinstate the full, pre-settlement amount of the debt. A reinstated debt has had no lasting change to the terms, so under FDRs own definition, no settlement exists yet FDR keeps the fee as earned in full and non-refundable (Section 5.a.i), renegotiates, tells me to start over, and charges another settlement fee on the same enrolled debt. When my funds ran short, FDR did not abandon the settlements closest to being done for me it abandoned the ones where it had not yet collected its own fee. When FDR voids a settlement that has already been paid and then charges again for the renegotiated settlement of the same debt, it effectively collects two fees for one debtsomething that the agreement does not permit anywhere.

The CFPB alleged that FDR charged advance fees in violation of the TSR, charged its full fee even when creditors merely stopped collection without a settlement, required consumers to negotiate their own settlements, misled consumers about its fees, and failed to disclose consumers rights to dedicated-account funds upon withdrawal. The order enjoins FDR from charging a fee on a Non-Settlement Outcome a debt FDR treats as resolved that was not settled with the creditor. My complaints 1 and 2 describe the same conduct already enjoined.

FDRs own contract defeats these fees

On the XXXX account alone, costs of $XXXX exceed the $XXXX enrolled amount by $XXXX squarely within the refund guarantee promised.

Complaint Against Bank of America Regarding Denial of XXXX Fraud Claim To Whom It May Concern : I am submitting this complaint against Bank of America regarding its refusal to help me get back my funds lost through a fraudulent XXXX transaction despite clear evidence that I was the victim of impersonation, deception, and criminal fraud. On XX/XX/year>, I received messages through XXXX from what appeared to be my friend 's XXXX XXXX legitimate account and phone number, XXXX. The messages requested urgent financial assistance. Because I personally know this individual and had communicated with him through this account previously, I had every reason to believe I was speaking directly with my friend. Relying on those representations and acting in good faith, I sent {$1900.00} through XXXX to XXXX XXXX, using the XXXX account registered under XXXX. Shortly after the transfer, I discovered that my friend 's XXXX account had been hacked and was being used by an unknown individual to impersonate him and solicit money from his contacts. I immediately realized that I had been deceived by a criminal actor who exploited a trusted relationship and a compromised communication platform. Following discovery of the fraud, I immediately notified Bank of America and submitted a fraud claim. I provided all information available to me regarding the impersonation scheme and the circumstances surrounding the transaction. Despite my prompt reporting and cooperation, Bank of America denied my claim and refused reimbursement. After receiving the bank 's denial, I reported the matter to the XXXX XXXX Police Department. The incident was documented under Police Report XXXX. XXXX, and the police investigation identified the crime as Theft by Deception. The report confirms that the perpetrator used my friend 's compromised XXXX account to impersonate him and fraudulently obtain money from individuals who reasonably believed they were communicating with a trusted contact. The bank 's position appears to be based solely on the fact that I physically initiated the transfer. However, that conclusion ignores the critical fact that my authorization was procured through fraud and criminal impersonation. I did not knowingly send money to a scammer, a stranger, or an unauthorized recipient. Rather, I intended to send money to a person whom I personally knew and trusted. The transaction occurred only because a third-party criminal successfully impersonated that individual through a hacked communications account. This distinction is significant. Consumers are routinely advised by XXXX and participating financial institutions to send money only to people they know and trust. In this case, I followed that guidance. I was attempting to assist someone I knew personally. The fraud occurred because a criminal actor compromised a trusted communication channel and exploited that relationship. The circumstances of this case demonstrate a growing consumer protection issue involving person-to-person payment platforms. Fraudsters increasingly gain access to legitimate communication accounts and impersonate trusted individuals, making it difficult for consumers to detect the deception. Under these circumstances, consumers may reasonably believe they are acting consistently with the warnings and guidance provided by payment platforms. Additionally, after my experience became known within my community, other individuals reported receiving similar fraudulent requests from the same compromised account. Fortunately, they were warned because of what happened to me and avoided becoming victims themselves. This further confirms that the scheme involved a broader pattern of impersonation and fraud rather than a voluntary transfer to a known scammer. I respectfully request that the CFPB review Bank of America 's handling of this matter and determine whether the bank conducted a reasonable investigation before denying my claim. Specifically, I request review of : - Whether Bank of America adequately considered the evidence of account compromise, impersonation, and theft by deception ; - Whether the investigation improperly focused only on the mechanical fact that I initiated the transfer while disregarding the fraudulent circumstances under which the authorization was obtained ; - Whether Bank of America fulfilled its consumer protection obligations in reviewing and responding to my fraud claim ; and - Whether additional measures are necessary to protect consumers who are victimized through impersonation schemes conducted over compromised communication accounts. As a result of this incident, I suffered a financial loss of {$1900.00}, which has not been recovered. Despite reporting the fraud promptly and providing supporting documentation, Bank of America has completely denied my claim and I have received no reimbursement. I respectfully request that Bank of America reopen and reconsider its decision and that the CFPB assist in facilitating a fair review of this matter. Thank you for your attention to this complaint. Unfair, Deceptive, or Abusive Acts or Practices ( UDAAP ) Goldman Sachs conduct may constitute an unfair or deceptive practice because : The alleged requirement is not clearly disclosed. The CFPB found that Goldman Sachs failed to properly investigate certain consumer disputes and that Apple and Goldman Sachs misled some consumers regarding interest-related payment plans. I respectfully request CFPB intervention and a full review of Goldman Sachs Apple Card servicing practices as they relate to residual interest disclosures and billing practices. Sincerely, XXXX XXXX

Equifax can not simply defer to XXXX when XXXX 's own basis for denying fraud has been disproven by XXXX XXXX. A consumer reporting agency has an independent obligation to assure maximum possible accuracy. Continuing to publish derogatory information after receiving evidence that undermines the furnisher 's conclusions is inconsistent with that obligation. Likewise, Upstart can not continue using a fraudulent XXXX XXXX account as evidence that I authorized this loan when XXXX XXXX itself has determined that I neither opened nor knew about that account. At this point, the continued furnishing and reporting of this account is not supported by competent evidence and renders the tradeline inaccurate, unreliable, and unverifiable. XXXX 's denial became untenable the moment XXXX Fargothe institution whose account XXXX relied upondetermined that account ending in XXXX was itself fraudulent. Consumer complaint narrative: I am disputing two add-on products the dealership financed into my Wells Fargo Auto loan , and Wells Fargo 's refusal to take responsibility for them. On XX/XX/XXXX, I purchased a XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX from XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX ( XXXX XXXX ). The dealer financed two add-on products into my loan : a GAP product ( {$1200.00} ) and a 3-year cosmetic/appearance protection coverage plan ( {$5400.00} ), for a combined {$6600.00}. The XXXX is XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX ( XXXX, NJ ). On XX/XX/XXXX - 23 days after purchase - I submitted a written cancellation request for both products, with no claims ever filed on either. XXXX ( {$1200.00} ) : Under New Jersey law the GAP free-look period is no less than 30 days, and cancelling within that period when no benefits have been provided entitles me to a full refund of the purchase price. I cancelled at day 23, so I am owed a full {$1200.00} refund. Cosmetic plan ( {$5400.00} ) : This was a 3-year coverage plan. No product or benefit was ever provided, and I have documentation confirming nothing was ever applied to the vehicle. I am therefore owed a full refund. At an absolute minimum I am owed a pro-rata refund of the unearned coverage, which after three weeks of a three-year term is nearly the entire purchase price. I created a documented certified-mail trail with return receipts : certified letters to XXXX XXXX XXXXXXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX and signed for, late XX/XX/XXXX ) ; a signed delivery confirmation from the XXXX dated XX/XX/XXXX ; and certified " Billing Discrepancies and Refund Request '' letters to Wells Fargo Auto at multiple addresses ( delivered and signed for on XX/XX/XXXX and XX/XX/XXXX ). I have also called Wells Fargo more than five times and emailed them the signed contract. Despite this, Wells Fargo told me only the GAP product appears in its system and that it has no record of the {$5400.00} cosmetic contract. After I emailed Wells Fargo the signed contract showing the {$5400.00} was rolled into the principal it financed, Wells Fargo still stated that only the dealer is responsible and directed me back to the dealer, who has not resolved this. Wells Fargo also states it sent a cancellation notice but can not confirm the cancellation. Wells Fargo financed this entire balance and continues to charge interest on the disputed {$6600.00}. [ As the holder of my retail installment contract, Wells Fargo is subject to the claims and defenses I can assert against the dealer under the FTC Holder Rule ( 16 CFR Part 433 ) and can not simply redirect me to an unresponsive dealer. ] I am asking Wells Fargo to : identify the full breakdown of add-on amounts financed into my principal ; trace and confirm the cancellation notice it says it sent ; accept and review the signed contract I provided ; open a formal escalation case and give me a tracking number ; and credit the unearned and undelivered amounts to my loan principal, backdated to my XX/XX/XXXX cancellation request, with an adjustment for the interest charged on these amounts.

Consumer complaint narrative: I am filing this complaint because JP Morgan Chase has now denied a legitimate billing dispute twice without ever examining the actual substance of my claim, and I am frankly appalled at how this has been handled. The disputed charge is {$590.00}, posted on or around XX/XX/year> to my account ending in XXXX, for a cash co-payment XXXX demanded on a XXXX award airline ticket. This is not a complaint about a price I simply disliked. It is a documented case of arbitrary, self-contradicting, and deceptive pricing by the merchant, and the evidence proving it has been submitted to the issuer and ignored. Below is exactly what happened, in the utmost detail : I held approximately XXXX points with XXXX ( another credit card ) and transferred them to XXXX XXXX at a XXXX ratio, giving me roughly XXXX XXXX. By XXXX 's own published valuation, those points were worth about {$620.00} if I were to book a ticket on their portal. However, I transferred them to XXXX ( who, according to various travel websites had a better point valuation ) for XXXX specific purpose : to book a round-trip flight from XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX The ordinary cash price for that exact itinerary, on those same airlines, was $ XXXX. I have screenshots documenting this. When I attempted to book that round trip as an award ticket on XXXX 's website, the merchant demanded ALL XXXX of my miles PLUS an additional {$1100.00} in cash for the same exact flights. Consider what that actually means : - Buying the ticket outright with cash : $ XXXX. - Booking the very same seats using miles : about {$620.00} worth of miles, XXXX {$1100.00} in cash, resulting in an effective total cost of roughly {$1700.00}. In other words, XXXX required me to surrender XXXX miles AND pay {$1100.00} ( more than double the cash price ) for a flight I could have simply purchased for $ XXXX. Redeeming my miles did not save me a single dollar ; it cost me far more than paying cash would have. That is the exact opposite of what an airline-miles program is represented to be, and it is the heart of why this is deceptive. At the same time, XXXX did not offer me the option of refunding my miles back to XXXX so I can at least book my ticket on their respective travel portal. This way, they effectively " trapped '' me into having to make a decision that I could have avoided. When I asked XXXX 's customer service to explain, the only answer I received was " dynamic pricing with partner airlines ''. That does not explain, and can not justify, charging a large cash premium far above the open-market cash fare for the same seats. In addition, this explanation was given to me verbally, through the phone, meaning that they carefully tried to avoid producing written documentation for it. Because the round-trip redemption was economically absurd, I booked the XXXX legs separately in an effort to find a way around the " trap '' to which they lead me with their deceptive advertising and arbitray pricing. The outbound leg ( XXXX to XXXX. Normal price $ XXXX ) redeemed for XXXX miles. The return leg ( XXXX to XXXX, a ticket worth again roughly $ XXXX in cash ) required only XXXX miles PLUS the {$590.00} cash charge I am now disputing. The merchant 's own back-to-back pricing contradicts itself : XXXX miles covered a ~ {$450.00} ticket, yet a comparable ~ {$500.00} ticket cost XXXX miles AND an extra {$590.00} in cash. There is no consistent, disclosed valuation that produces both of those numbers. I received no additional product, service, or benefit for that {$590.00} ; I was charged it solely because of the merchant 's undisclosed and self-contradicting valuation of its own currency. In addition to all of that, the fact that I could use the XXXX miles on XXXX separate flights for a total of approximately {$700.00} ( including the taxes I paid for the first of the XXXX flights which was covered with XXXX miles ) proves beyond any doubt the arbitrary and absurd demand of XXXX for {$1100.00} on top of my XXXX, which they presented as the price to me as the option for booking a single round-trip ticket. This is not buyer 's remorse over a price I knowingly agreed to. It is a documented case of a merchant assigning arbitrary, inconsistent, and undisclosed value to its own currency in order to extract cash above the market fare. I relied on the represented value of these miles when I transferred them, and that reliance was defeated entirely by the merchant 's conduct. Complaint Regarding Mishandled Account Closure And Failure To Provide Adequate Review To whom it may concern, I am submitting this complaint regarding _Bank and its handling of my account closure and subsequent attempts to seek clarification and resolution. This created an absurd loop where the branch directs me to the call center and the call center directs me back to the branch, with no one taking responsibility for actually reviewing my situation. My key concerns : I followed the script, used precise language, and explicitly requested a manual review of the decision. Instead of reviewing or documenting the specifics of my case, multiple representatives hid behind the banks broad right to close accounts, effectively allowing an automated decision to be final without oversight. My request to escalate to a supervisor did not result in any additional review or explanation. The supervisor repeated the same scripted response and refused to deviate from it, even when I pointed out that I had followed all instructions and was simply asking for a real, documented review. The banks own employees placed me into a circular loop. The branch told me they had no authority and that I must call the support line. The support line, including a supervisor, then told me to go back to the branch. At no point did anyone take ownership of the issue, provide a clear explanation, or offer a path to resolution. This is not merely an individual representatives mistake ; it reflects a systemic design where customers can be endlessly passed around without accountability. Based on the statements I received, it appears that the bank is relying heavily on automated systems to flag and close accounts, then using generic policy language to avoid conducting a human review when a customer challenges the result. This creates a system where there is effectively no due process or meaningful appeal for consumers. I understand that financial institutions may reserve the right to close accounts. My complaint is not simply that my account was closed, but that the bank : Refused to perform a genuine, documented manual review despite my explicit, repeated requests. Failed to provide any clear, specific reason or evidence for the action beyond generic policy language. Structured its support process in a way that left me trapped between the branch and the call center, with each side disclaiming responsibility. I am requesting that the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau : Require the bank to conduct and document a manual review of my case, including the specific reasons and data that led to the closure. Consumer complaint narrative: I have been a Marcus savings account customer since XXXX. In XX/XX/XXXX, I became aware of a promotion offering a {$1500.00} bonus for depositing {$100000.00} in new funds and maintaining those funds in a Marcus account for 90 days. Because I already had an existing Marcus savings account, I contacted Marcus before moving any money to confirm that existing customers were eligible to participate in the promotion. After making that inquiry, I transferred {$100000.00} in new funds from XXXX into my Marcus savings account and maintained those funds for the required period. After more than 90 days had passed, I checked my account and discovered that the promised bonus had not been credited. When I contacted Marcus, I was informed that I was ineligible because I had not completed a separate enrollment process. The representative further stated that many customers had encountered the same issue. I escalated the matter to a supervisor, but again was told only that I had not enrolled and therefore would not receive the bonus. My complaint is not simply that I missed a procedural step. My concern is that the enrollment requirement appears to function as a barrier that predictably disqualifies consumers who otherwise satisfy the substantive requirements of the promotion. Marcus representatives themselves acknowledged that many customers fail to complete this step. If large numbers of consumers are being denied an advertised bonus for the same reason, that raises serious concerns about whether the requirement is being communicated effectively and transparently. As an existing customer, I was not opening a new account. I was responding to a promotional offer that required a deposit of new funds and a 90-day holding period. In that context, the term " enrollment '' was not presented to me as a critical requirement carrying a {$1500.00} consequence. The denial of a {$1500.00} bonus based solely on a missed procedural step is particularly troubling where the consumer has fully satisfied the economic substance of the promotion by depositing and maintaining {$100000.00} in new funds for the required period. What concerns me most is that the enrollment requirement serves no apparent substantive purpose. Marcus already knows when a customer deposits qualifying new funds and maintains those funds for the required period. If enrollment were truly intended to ensure informed participation rather than to create a procedural hurdle, Marcus could easily implement safeguards such as automatic prompts, warning messages before qualifying transfers, follow-up reminders, account notifications, or other mechanisms that would alert customers that an additional action is required. Instead, customers can deposit substantial sums, maintain those balances for months, and only later discover that they have been disqualified from receiving the advertised bonus. The practical effect of the current process is that XXXX receives the benefit of qualifying deposits while retaining the ability to deny the advertised bonus based on a procedural requirement that many consumers apparently overlook. Based on my experience and the number of similar complaints publicly reported by other consumers, this does not appear to be an isolated incident but rather a recurring source of consumer confusion. I have seen consumer complaints about this issue on CFPB, XXXX XXXX XXXX, XXXX, XXXX and other financial sites and social media. I attempted to resolve this matter directly with XXXX. I submitted a written complaint and sought reconsideration of my eligibility. Rather than addressing the substance of my concerns, Marcus repeatedly relied on the same response : that I had not enrolled. The bank did not address whether the enrollment requirement was adequately disclosed, whether the promotional process is reasonably understandable to existing customers, or whether recurring consumer confusion suggests deficiencies in the design or administration of the promotion. I respectfully request that this matter be reviewed to determine whether Marcus 's promotional practices, disclosures, and complaint-handling procedures are consistent with principles of fair and transparent treatment of consumers. I also request that Marcus reconsider its decision and honor the {$1500.00} promotional bonus based on my deposit of {$100000.00} in new funds and my compliance with the 90-day holding requirement. Thank you for your attention to this complaint.

I am not refusing to pay ; I am requesting the documentation I am legally entitled to before continuing payments or discussing any settlement options. '' USPS tracking confirms delivery on XX/XX/XXXX. Despite receiving my revocation and accounting request, Rodenburg withdrew funds from my bank account on XX/XX/XXXX. This withdrawal was made using a remotely created check ( RCC ), which I did not authorize. I have never authorized the use of RCCs, and I revoked authorization for any automatic withdrawals before this debit occurred. The withdrawal was therefore unauthorized. Rodenburg has been using RCCs to withdraw funds monthly, but I was not informed that these were RCCs, and I did not consent to this method. I believed these were ACH withdrawals until I contacted my bank. RCCs still require consumer authorization under UCC 3403, and creating a check using my account number without my authorization is an unauthorized electronic debit. Rodenburg also failed to provide any accounting for over XXXX years, despite taking monthly payments. When I requested accounting on XX/XX/XXXX, they did not provide it before continuing collection activity. They later claimed they mailed it on the XXXX, but this was after the unauthorized withdrawal, and I still have not received it. Under FDCPA 809 ( b ), once a consumer disputes a debt or requests validation/accounting, the collector must cease collection activity until the requested information is provided. I already manually paid via their website on XX/XX/XXXX because I knew they'd received my letter, so in effect, I paid twice. When I contacted the firm, the attorney stated that my revocation did not apply because they were using RCCs instead of ACH. This is incorrect. Consumers are not required to list every possible withdrawal method in a revocation. Revoking authorization for automatic withdrawals applies to any method of electronically debiting a bank account. The attorneys statement was misleading and appears intended to avoid compliance with federal law. I am requesting that the CFPB investigate the following issues : Unauthorized XXXX withdrawal after written revocation, Failure to provide accounting before continuing collection, Failure to provide accounting for over XXXX years, Misrepresentation of consumer rights, Continued collection activity after written dispute, Hostile or misleading communication by the attorney XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX ). Consumer complaint narrative: I, XXXX XXXX, owner of XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, submit this complaint against Wells Fargo Bank N.A for its wrongful handling of a XXXX chargeback dispute ( reason code 10.4 - other fraud, card absent environment ) The financial harm to my business resulted from two distinct failures ; Wells Fargo 's failure to follow XXXX XXXX mandated dispute investigation procedures for card-not-present fraud and XXXX XXXX automatic deduction of transaction processing fees and dispute fees, which I was charged despite the dispute being incorrectly decided against me. Wells Fargo 's mishandling of this dispute led to an incorrect chargeback decision that caused direct and material financial harm to my business. MERCHANT ROLE IN THE TRANSACTION XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX is a registered merchant operating on the XXXX XXXX platform, which uses XXXX as its payment processor. The following describes how transactions are processes in the environment, and why the merchant bears no responsibility for cardholder registration, verification or authorization. XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX ( merchant ) has no involvement in bidder registration and does not handle, enter, or store any card credentials. The merchant does not perform and is not authorized to perform any verification, authentication, or authorization of payments. All cardholder data is transmitted directly and exclusively from the cardholder to XXXX. The merchant is never is possession of this information. Charges are processed and authorized automatically through XXXX 's secure, tokenized payment system entirely without merchant involvement. The merchant 's only visibility into a customer 's account is the name, billing and shipping addresses and last four digits of the card number - information already verified and authenticated by XXXX and the issuing bank prior to authorization. FACTS OF THE TRANSACTION On XX/XX/year> bidder XXXX XXXX registered on the XXXX XXXX platform. He purchased multiple lots of fine jewelry totaling {$3800.00}. Following the auction XXXX XXXX contacted XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX via email and requested that the items be shipped to the shipping and billing address on file with the XXXX XXXX platform. A shipping and insurance fee of {$120.00}. XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX fulfilled the order in the full compliance with platform procedures. The goods were delivered to the verified billing and shipping address provided by the buyer. The billing and shipping address were identical. On XX/XX/year> XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX received notice of a chargeback dispute for the full amounts of {$3800.00} and {$120.00}. All relevant evidence was promptly submitted to XXXX in response to the dispute. WELLS FARGO 'S DISPUTE DECISION ; On XX/XX/year> Wells Fargo issued its dispute decision in favor of the cardholder. The bank 's stated rationale was as follows : ( Our center has certified that this is an unauthorized transaction. The merchant provided no proof that our cardholder authorized the disputed transaction. Neither the name nor the address provided by the merchant matches our cardholder 's profile. The cardholder denies participation in the transaction, engagement with the merchant, or receipt of services. We have met all technical and certification requirements. The account was closed, placed on the exception file, and reported to XXXX as having been used fraudulently. Our cardholder is due full credit ) Wells Fargo categorized the dispute under XXXX Reason Code 10.4 ( other fraud card absent environment ) GROUNDS FOR COMPLAINT a ) The merchant XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX can not provide authorization proof. Wells Fargo 's decision faults the merchant for failing to provide proof that the cardholder authorized the transaction. This requirement is factually and procedurally impossible to satisfy. As described above, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX has no role in the authorization process. The merchant never handles card credentials, does not interact with XXXX or Wells Fargo 's authorization system, and is not provided with any authorization codes, CVV results, or AVS response coded. The information merchant submitted- the buyer 's name, billing and shipping address is the information that XXXX presented to Wells Fargo during the authorization request. If that information did not match Wells Fargo 's records, the bank had both the ability and the obligation to decline the transaction at the point of authorization. WELLS FARGO FAILED ITS DUTY AT THE POINT OF AUTHORIZATION Under XXXX Rules and XXXX Product and Service Rules, when an authorization request is submitted, the issuing bank is responsible for verifying cardholder credentials including name, billing address, and card validation codes against its own records. If those credentials do not match the issuer is required to return a decline response, such as Response Code 93 ( transaction can not be completed ) By approving the XXXX tokenized request, Wells Fargo effectively certified that the credentials presented were valid and acceptable. The bank can not now claim that the name and address did not match its records, while simultaneously having approved the transaction. These positions are mutually contradictory. The merchant had no mechanism to perform these checks and no access to the results of any AVS or CVV verification. Chargeback liability can not be assigned to a party who is structurally excluded from the authorization process. ASSIGNEMENT OF CHARGEBACK LIABILITY VIOLATES CARD NETWORK RULES XXXX XXXX own rules prohibit issuers from assigning chargeback liability to merchant under the following circumstances ; Merchants did not process or authorize the transaction. Merchant relied on processor level ( XXXX ) authentication and tokenization. The issuer approved the transaction through its own authorization system. FINANCIAL HARM FROM INCORRECTLY ASSESSED FEES In addition to the chargeback amount itself, XXXX automatically deducted transaction processing fees and dispute fees from my account in connection with these chargebacks. These fees were assessed despite the fact that the dispute was incorrectly decided and the merchant bore no responsibility. RELIEF REQUESTED XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX respectfully requests that the CFPB take the actions ; Direct Wells Fargo to reverse both chargebacks ( {$3800.00} and {$120.00} ), Direct Wells Fargo to reimburse all XXXX dispute fees assessed to XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX as a result of this incorrectly decided dispute. I certify that the information in this complaint is true and accurate to the best of my knowledge. All supporting documentation will be submitted to this complaint. XXXX ( XXXX ) XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XX/XX/year> 2026

I am filing this complaint regarding a personal loan in the amount of approximately {$47000.00} and an origination fee of {$3000.00} that was charged after I attempted to cancel the transaction. On XX/XX/year>, I electronically signed a personal loan agreement. The agreement contained a provision stating that I could cancel my application without fee or penalty prior to funding if I provided sufficient advance notice to stop the funding process. At the time I signed the agreement, I was not informed that funding would be initiated automatically and immediately as part of the lender 's internal process. Believing that I still had the ability to exercise the contractual cancellation provision, I subsequently contacted the lender and requested cancellation. It was only after I attempted to cancel that I was informed by the lender that funding had already been initiated automatically and that cancellation was therefore no longer possible. As a result, I became responsible for an origination fee despite my effort to cancel the transaction and send back the funds immediately, and despite the contract 's representation that cancellation before funding was permitted. My concern is that the lender 's process effectively prevents consumers from exercising the cancellation right described in the agreement. Consumers are told they may cancel before funding if they provide sufficient advance notice, yet funding is initiated automatically without a meaningful opportunity to provide that notice. I did not learn that funding had already been initiated until after I contacted the lender to cancel. I am requesting that the lender review this matter, refund or waive the origination fee, and provide a written explanation of how consumers can realistically exercise the contractual cancellation right described in the agreement when funding is automatically initiated immediately after signing. I also request that any reporting related to this account accurately reflect that the origination fee and underlying obligation are disputed while this matter is under review.
Product: Payday loan, title loan, personal loan, or advance loan

b'In a marketing letter received on XXXX for a VA-Guaranteed Cash Out Loan Offer (Reservation # XXXX XXXX XXXX), there is direct evidence of false and/or misleading advertising by New Day USA. The first three sentences of the letter state:
"Prices on everything have gone up and up. The good news? So have home values."

As an example, we paid just over $XXXX for our home in XXXX. I now see comparable homes on the market for XXXX, $XXXX, and even as low as $XXXX, with some of these homes being openly listed for 7-10 months without sale, and several showing multiple price reductions to attract buyers. This type of misleading information is unjust and unfair to the public at large, and is the same type of predatory tactic that led to one of the worst financial disasters in recorded history. Consumer complaint narrative: Dear Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, I respectfully submit this rebuttal to TitleMax of Nevada, Inc.s latest response. I do not consider this matter resolved and respectfully request that the CFPB continue its review and investigation. After reviewing TitleMaxs latest response and the supporting documentation they have chosen to produce, my concerns have not been resolved. Instead, the records produced by TitleMax raise additional questions regarding notice, account access, payoff information, servicing practices, repossession procedures, and the completeness of their disclosures. At this stage, many of the concerns raised in this complaint are no longer based solely upon my recollection of events. They arise directly from TitleMaxs own records, timelines, statements, and explanations. As additional information has been produced, new inconsistencies have emerged rather than existing concerns being resolved. GOOD-FAITH EFFORTS TO FULLY RESOLVE THE ACCOUNT TitleMax continues to portray this matter as a simple payment default. That characterization omits critical facts. Throughout the life of this account, I experienced ongoing difficulties accessing and managing the account due to the account-access issues described throughout this complaint. I was unable to reliably access the online portal, independently verify balances, review account information, obtain payoff information, or effectively service the account through the systems that TitleMax claims were available to me. As a result, I was deprived of the ability to independently monitor and manage the account. Prior to the repossession process, I had not received effective notice that would have allowed me to meaningfully evaluate my options or independently determine what was required to fully resolve the account. Instead, TitleMax contacted me directly and informed me that repossession activity was being pursued and that my vehicle was at risk of being taken. Upon receiving that communication, I did not ignore the situation. I immediately sought information necessary to permanently resolve the matter. Most importantly, I did not ask what amount was necessary to simply bring the account current. I specifically requested the amount necessary to satisfy the obligation in full, recover my title, and completely resolve the account. My objective was not to make another periodic payment, extend the loan, or continue the lending relationship. My objective was to obtain a full payoff amount so that the debt could be satisfied, the title could be released, and the matter could be concluded permanently. This distinction is important. A payment intended only to bring an account current generates additional future payments, additional interest, and continued obligations. By contrast, a full payoff would have completely resolved the account and terminated any future obligations associated with the loan. Despite specifically requesting the information necessary to fully satisfy the obligation, I was not provided with clear, consistent, and reliable payoff information. Instead, I received conflicting figures and inconsistent information regarding the amount required to fully resolve the account. As a result, I was deprived of a meaningful opportunity to evaluate my options and satisfy the debt based upon accurate information. The facts remain that : I was unable to reliably access and service the account through the online portal. TitleMax contacted me regarding repossession activity. I immediately sought the information necessary to prevent repossession and fully satisfy the obligation. I specifically requested payoff information rather than merely a catch-up amount. I was provided inconsistent information regarding the amount necessary to accomplish that goal. I subsequently made a substantial payment toward the account. The vehicle was nevertheless repossessed. The issue is therefore not whether I was willing to pay. The issue is whether I was provided accurate information, meaningful account access, effective notice, and a fair opportunity to satisfy the obligation in full before losing a vehicle that I had purchased outright. ACCOUNT ACCESS ISSUES REMAIN UNRESOLVED TitleMax attempts to dismiss my concerns regarding account access by suggesting that I incorrectly saved my phone number in a password manager. That explanation does not accurately reflect the issue. The issue was never a simple password-manager error. I have worked extensively with computers for most of my life and have received formal technical training, including information technology certification. Based upon that experience, I do not find TitleMaxs explanation that these access failures were caused solely by a phone number being incorrectly saved within a personal password manager to be a sufficient explanation for the issues I experienced. As a practical matter, consumers do not possess the ability to independently modify account-level authentication credentials, customer-profile information, account-recovery records, or other backend account data without intervention from the company maintaining those systems. Regardless of the underlying technical cause, the outcome remained the same : I was unable to reliably access the account, verify balances, review notices, obtain account information, or independently manage the loan through the online portal. Because I remained locked out of the account, I was forced to rely upon TitleMax representatives for information regarding balances, payoff amounts, account status, repayment options, and servicing of the account. It was during those interactions that I received conflicting and inconsistent information regarding the amount necessary to resolve the account. Had I been able to access the account as intended, independently verify balances, review notices, obtain payoff information, and manage the loan through the online portal, many of the disputes presently before the CFPB may never have arisen. TITLEMAXS OWN TIMELINE RAISES QUESTIONS TitleMaxs response relies heavily upon an alleged Opportunity to Enter into a Repayment Plan ( OERP ) notice. However, according to TitleMaxs own response : I made a payment of {$1100.00} on XX/XX/year>. The tracking information TitleMax produced reflects final delivery activity occurring on XX/XX/year>. Even accepting TitleMaxs version of events as true, their own records establish that I could not have reviewed or acted upon the contents of the alleged notice before making that payment. Accordingly, TitleMax can not reasonably argue that I knowingly ignored repayment options contained within a notice that, according to their own evidence, was not allegedly delivered until after I made a substantial payment toward the account. This inconsistency remains unexplained. DISABILITY-RELATED IMPACT An additional concern involves the disproportionate impact that these events have had upon me as an individual with a documented disability. At the time the vehicle was repossessed, the vehicle displayed a handicap placard and contained disability-related support items, including a back brace and seat-support equipment. TitleMax therefore had direct knowledge, or at minimum direct visual evidence, that the vehicle was being used in connection with disability-related mobility needs. The repossession has had consequences extending beyond the loss of transportation. In addition to losing access to the vehicle itself, personal property associated with my disability remained inside the vehicle at the time of repossession. To date, those items have not been returned to me. The loss of access to both the vehicle and these support items has substantially increased the hardship resulting from this matter. Because of my disability, reliable remote access to account information was especially important. Online servicing systems, account-recovery systems, and telephone servicing were not merely conveniences. They were essential tools that allowed me to independently access and manage my financial obligations. TitleMaxs repeated suggestion that I could simply visit a storefront location does not address the underlying issue that I was unable to independently manage the account through the systems they provided. The subsequent loss of my vehicle further compounded those difficulties by reducing my mobility, limiting my ability to work, impairing my ability to attend appointments, and making it substantially more difficult to address financial obligations and daily responsibilities. For these reasons, I respectfully request that CFPB consider not only the financial impact of this matter, but also the disproportionate burden imposed by the loss of transportation, loss of account access, and loss of disability-related personal property.

Midland responded by letter dated XX/XX/XXXX. The response states that Midland reviewed its information and concluded that its records are accurate. Midland provided some documentation, including an account summary, XXXX XXXXXXXX XXXX XXXX XXXXXXXX XXXX statements, and a sale notice. However, Midlands response does not fully validate the account or resolve the issues raised in my debt validation request. The documents provided do not include a signed agreement or application bearing my signature. Midland also did not provide the actual bill of sale, purchase agreement, account-level sale schedule, or complete assignment documents proving that this specific account was included in a valid transfer to Midland Credit Management XXXX Midlands response states that the account was purchased on XX/XX/XXXX. However, the XXXX sale notice included in the response states that the account was sold to Midland on XX/XX/XXXX. Midland did not explain this discrepancy. These conflicting dates raise concerns about the accuracy and completeness of the ownership and transfer documentation. The response also does not provide a complete payment history from account opening through charge-off and sale. Midland provided selected statements, but selected statements are not the same as a complete payment history. They do not fully explain all charges, fees, interest, credits, payments, adjustments, charge-off amount, or the final balance Midland claims is owed. Midland states the current balance is {$3100.00}. The documents provided do not include a complete itemized calculation showing how the balance was determined, how it reached the claimed sale amount, or how Midland verified the balance as accurate. A balance summary is not a full itemized balance calculation. The response also does not provide complete documentation showing Midlands authority to furnish this account to consumer reporting agencies. If Midland is collecting and furnishing this account, Midland should be able to provide complete account-level documentation proving ownership, assignment, balance accuracy, and reporting authority.
